subject: Dermatology
front: What are the three main layers of the skin and their embryological origin?
back: Epidermis (ectoderm), Dermis (mesoderm), and Hypodermis/subcutis (mesoderm).

subject: Dermatology
front: Despite both residing in the epidermis, what is the embryological origin of melanocytes vs Langerhans cells?
back: Melanocytes arise from neural crest cells; Langerhans cells arise from mesoderm (bone marrow-derived).

subject: Dermatology
front: What are the two layers of the dermis and its collagen type?
back: Papillary dermis (superficial) and Reticular dermis (deeper); the dermis has dense irregular collagen.

subject: Dermatology
front: List the 5 layers of the epidermis, from deepest to most superficial.
back: Stratum basale, stratum spinosum, stratum granulosum, stratum lucidum, stratum corneum.

subject: Dermatology
front: Where is the stratum lucidum found, and what does it contain?
back: Only in palms and soles; contains refractile granules of eleidin.

subject: Dermatology
front: What structures/proteins are in the stratum granulosum, and which conditions relate to them?
back: Odland (lamellar) bodies and keratohyaline granules; contains filaggrin (deficiency causes ichthyosis vulgaris); also associated with asteatotic eczema.

subject: Dermatology
front: What is the key epidermal adhesion molecule in the stratum spinosum ("acanthocytes"), and which diseases cause acantholysis there?
back: Desmoglein (DSG); acantholysis occurs in Pemphigus (anti-DSG antibodies), HSV, Hailey-Hailey disease, and Darier disease (the latter two via defective calcium-ATPase pumps).

subject: Dermatology
front: Which calcium pump gene is defective in Hailey-Hailey disease vs Darier disease?
back: Hailey-Hailey: ATP2C1 (Ca-ATPase pump); Darier disease: ATP2A2 (Ca-ATPase/SERCA2 pump).

subject: Dermatology
front: Which antigen-presenting epidermal cell resides in the stratum spinosum?
back: Langerhans cells (APC).

subject: Dermatology
front: What two epidermal layers together make up the ''Malpighian layer''?
back: Stratum basale + stratum spinosum.

subject: Dermatology
front: What immunohistochemical markers identify melanocytes (stratum basale)?
back: S-100, HMB-45, Melan-A.

subject: Dermatology
front: What markers identify Merkel cells, and what malignancy is associated?
back: CK20 positive, CK7 negative; associated with Merkel cell carcinoma (colon cancer can show a similar CK20+/CK7- pattern).

subject: Dermatology
front: What is the epidermal melanin unit ratio?
back: 1 melanocyte : 36 keratinocytes.

subject: Dermatology
front: What is the normal epidermal turnover time, and how does it change in psoriasis?
back: Normal turnover is ~56 days; reduced to 5-6 days in psoriasis due to accelerated proliferation.

subject: Dermatology
front: What are the characteristic ultrastructural/immunohistochemical findings in Langerhans Cell Histiocytosis?
back: Birbeck granules (tennis-racket shaped), CD207 (langerin), S-100 positivity, and CD1a positivity.

subject: Dermatology
front: What is the Hand-Schüller-Christian triad?
back: Proptosis, Diabetes insipidus, and Calvarial (lytic) skull lesions — a form of Langerhans Cell Histiocytosis.

subject: Dermatology
front: What type of secretion do sebaceous glands use?
back: Holocrine secretion.

subject: Dermatology
front: Are eccrine and apocrine sweat glands associated with hair follicles?
back: Eccrine glands are NOT associated with hair follicles; apocrine glands ARE associated with hair follicles (found at groin/axilla, and are responsible for body odour).

subject: Dermatology
front: What are the three stages of Miliaria, based on level of sweat duct obstruction?
back: Miliaria crystallina (intraepidermal sweat duct, most superficial), Miliaria rubra (reabsorptive sweat duct), Miliaria profunda (deeper, at the secretory coil).

subject: Dermatology
front: List the ectopic sebaceous glands and their locations.
back: Fordyce spots (lips), Montgomery tubercles (areola/breast), Meibomian and Zeis glands (eyelids), Tyson's glands (prepuce).

subject: Dermatology
front: List the modified apocrine glands and their locations.
back: Mammary glands (breast), Moll's glands (eyelids), Ceruminous glands (external auditory canal).

subject: Dermatology
front: What two conditions arise from apocrine gland pathology, and how do they differ?
back: Fox-Fordyce disease (apocrine duct occlusion causing pruritic papules) and Hidradenitis Suppurativa (chronic secondary inflammation of apocrine glands leading to discharging sinuses).

subject: Dermatology
front: Differentiate hyperkeratosis, parakeratosis, and orthokeratosis, with associated conditions.
back: Hyperkeratosis = increased keratin/thickness (Psoriasis, Lichen Planus); Parakeratosis = retained nuclei in stratum corneum (Psoriasis, chronic eczema, actinic keratosis, SCC); Orthokeratosis = hyperkeratosis WITHOUT parakeratosis (Lichen Planus).

subject: Dermatology
front: What is dyskeratosis, and which conditions show it?
back: Premature/abnormal keratinization of individual keratinocytes; seen in Darier's disease, actinic keratosis, and SCC.

subject: Dermatology
front: Contrast hypergranulosis and agranulosis with their associated conditions.
back: Hypergranulosis (thickened granular layer) occurs in Lichen Planus, producing Wickham's striae; Agranulosis (absent granular layer) occurs in Psoriasis.

subject: Dermatology
front: Differentiate spongiosis and acanthosis.
back: Spongiosis = intercellular epidermal edema, seen in acute eczema; Acanthosis = epidermal thickening, seen in Psoriasis.

subject: Dermatology
front: What is ''ballooning degeneration'' and where is it seen?
back: Intracellular edema of keratinocytes; seen in HSV infection.

subject: Dermatology
front: What is acantholysis, and which conditions show it?
back: Loss of intercellular cohesion between keratinocytes; seen in Pemphigus, SSSS, HSV, Hailey-Hailey disease, and Darier disease.

subject: Dermatology
front: What is Munro's microabscess (cell type and disease)?
back: Neutrophilic collections within the stratum corneum, seen in Psoriasis.

subject: Dermatology
front: What is Pautrier's microabscess (cell type and disease)?
back: Collections of lymphocytes within the epidermis, seen in Mycosis Fungoides/Cutaneous T-cell Lymphoma.

subject: Dermatology
front: What are Civatte bodies, and what infection is their associated disease linked to?
back: Apoptotic keratinocytes seen in Lichen Planus; LP is associated with Hepatitis C infection (Councilman bodies are the analogous hepatic apoptotic bodies seen in viral hepatitis).

subject: Dermatology
front: What is the earliest histological change in psoriasis?
back: Thinning of the suprapapillary epidermal plates.

subject: Dermatology
front: List the characteristic histological findings in psoriasis.
back: Parakeratosis, hyperkeratosis, agranulosis, Munro's microabscess (in stratum corneum), spongiform pustules of Kogoj (spinous/granular layer), club-shaped rete ridges, and dilated papillary dermal vessels with surrounding inflammation.

subject: Dermatology
front: List the characteristic histological findings in Lichen Planus.
back: Orthokeratosis with hypergranulosis (Wickham's striae), Civatte bodies, Max-Joseph space (basal cell degeneration/cleft), and a band-like (lichenoid) lymphocytic infiltrate at the dermo-epidermal junction.

subject: Dermatology
front: What immune markers/cytokines are elevated in psoriasis pathogenesis?
back: TNF-alpha, IL-6, CRP, and HLA-B27 association.

subject: Dermatology
front: What is the immune mechanism underlying Lichen Planus?
back: T-cell mediated (CD8+ cytotoxic T cells) causing interface dermatitis.

subject: Dermatology
front: What causes urticarial wheals histologically?
back: Dermal edema.

subject: Dermatology
front: How do you differentiate purpura from erythema using diascopy?
back: Purpura (due to RBC extravasation) does NOT blanch on diascopy; Erythema (due to vasodilation) DOES blanch on diascopy.

subject: Dermatology
front: Besides purpura, name other related vascular/hemorrhagic skin lesion types.
back: Abscess, petechiae, purpura, and ecchymosis.

subject: Dermatology
front: What are the classic site/scale/nail features of plaque psoriasis?
back: Extensor surfaces with silvery scales; nail changes include irregular pitting, the oil-droplet sign, and subungual hyperkeratosis.

subject: Dermatology
front: What is the "pencil-in-cup" deformity, and with which psoriatic condition is it associated?
back: A radiographic finding of erosion of the distal phalanx (cup) with tapering of the adjacent bone (pencil); seen in psoriatic arthritis mutilans.

subject: Dermatology
front: What is the most common joint pattern affected in psoriatic arthritis?
back: DIP joints most commonly, typically as an oligoarthritis.

subject: Dermatology
front: What is inverse (flexural) psoriasis, and how does it differ from plaque psoriasis?
back: It involves flexor surfaces/skin folds rather than extensors, and characteristically shows NO scales.

subject: Dermatology
front: What are the grattage test, Berkley membrane, and Auspitz sign in psoriasis?
back: Gentle scraping of a psoriatic scale (grattage test) first reveals a thin membrane (Berkley membrane); further scraping produces pinpoint bleeding (Auspitz sign), due to thinned suprapapillary plates over dilated capillaries.

subject: Dermatology
front: What is the Koebner phenomenon (isomorphic response), and in which 3 conditions is it classically seen?
back: Development of new lesions at sites of trauma; classically seen in Lichen Planus, Psoriasis (which can also show "reverse" Koebner), and Vitiligo.

subject: Dermatology
front: What is "pseudo-Koebner phenomenon," and in which conditions is it seen?
back: New lesions at trauma sites due to auto-inoculation (not a true isomorphic response); seen in viral warts and molluscum contagiosum.

subject: Dermatology
front: What is the Woronoff ring in psoriasis?
back: A pale halo/ring around a psoriatic plaque, caused by local prostaglandin (PG) release.

subject: Dermatology
front: What triggers guttate psoriasis, and what is its treatment?
back: Preceded by an upper respiratory tract infection (Group A Streptococcus); treated with macrolides.

subject: Dermatology
front: How is erythrodermic psoriasis defined (BSA), and how is it treated?
back: Psoriasis involving >90% body surface area; treated with Methotrexate (MTX).

subject: Dermatology
front: What typically precedes pustular psoriasis, and what is the eponym for its generalized form?
back: A history of steroid withdrawal; the generalized/diffuse form is called Von Zumbusch disease.

subject: Dermatology
front: What is impetigo herpetiformis, and how is it treated?
back: A pustular psoriasis variant occurring in pregnancy; treated with systemic steroids.

subject: Dermatology
front: Which HLA types and cytokines are associated with psoriasis pathogenesis?
back: HLA-Cw6 and HLA-B27; cytokines TNF-alpha, IL-17, and IL-23.

subject: Dermatology
front: List drugs/factors known to worsen or trigger psoriasis.
back: Lithium, Chloroquine, Beta-blockers, NSAIDs, systemic Steroids, Alcohol, and Smoking.

subject: Dermatology
front: Outline psoriasis treatment stepwise by body surface area (BSA) involvement.
back: <10% BSA: topical steroids. >10% BSA: phototherapy (PUVA or NB-UVB at 311 nm), stepping up to Methotrexate (MTX) if needed.

subject: Dermatology
front: How are psoriatic arthritis and erythrodermic psoriasis treated?
back: Methotrexate (MTX).

subject: Dermatology
front: How is pustular psoriasis treated, and what precaution is needed with this drug?
back: Acitretin (a retinoid); pregnancy must be avoided for 3 years after stopping due to teratogenicity.

subject: Dermatology
front: Match the biologic drug classes used in psoriasis to their targets: Ixekizumab/Secukinumab; Risankizumab/Guselkumab/Tildrakizumab; Ustekinumab; Apremilast; Tofacitinib.
back: Ixekizumab & Secukinumab = IL-17 inhibitors; Risankizumab, Guselkumab & Tildrakizumab = IL-23 inhibitors; Ustekinumab = IL-12/IL-23 inhibitor; Apremilast = PDE4 inhibitor; Tofacitinib = JAK1/3 inhibitor.

subject: Dermatology
front: What are the classic "6 P's" of Lichen Planus?
back: Pruritic, Purple, Planar, Polygonal, Papules, Plaques.

subject: Dermatology
front: Where does Lichen Planus classically occur, and what infection is it associated with?
back: Flexural surfaces; associated with Hepatitis C infection.

subject: Dermatology
front: Describe Wickham's striae, and how do they differ from oral candidiasis plaques?
back: Lacy, reticular white lines seen in oral LP lesions; they cannot be wiped off (unlike oral candidiasis, which can be).

subject: Dermatology
front: What drugs/exposures can trigger a lichenoid eruption resembling Lichen Planus?
back: ACE inhibitors, Beta-blockers, Chloroquine, and dental mercury (Hg) amalgam.

subject: Dermatology
front: What is the treatment for Lichen Planus?
back: Topical steroids.

subject: Dermatology
front: What are the characteristic dermoscopic and nail findings in Lichen Nitidus?
back: Dermoscopy shows the "pup-tent sign"; nails may show pterygium.

subject: Dermatology
front: What is the characteristic histopathological appearance of Lichen Nitidus?
back: "Claw clutching a ball" appearance — elongated rete ridges appear to clutch a dermal granulomatous infiltrate.

subject: Dermatology
front: What are the key clinical features of Pityriasis Rubra Pilaris?
back: Palmoplantar keratoderma, perifollicular involvement, and characteristic "islands of sparing" of normal skin within affected areas.

subject: Dermatology
front: What is the characteristic histological pattern seen in PRP?
back: A "checkerboard pattern" — alternating orthokeratosis and parakeratosis.

subject: Dermatology
front: Besides PRP, name two other causes of palmoplantar keratoderma mentioned in the notes.
back: Type 2 Tyrosinemia and Arsenic exposure.

subject: Dermatology
front: What is erythema nodosum, and what are its major causes?
back: A nodular, tender panniculitis; major causes include Histoplasma infection, Tuberculosis, Sarcoidosis, Behçet's disease, and IBD.

subject: Dermatology
front: What is Löfgren syndrome?
back: An acute presentation of sarcoidosis featuring hilar lymphadenopathy, erythema nodosum, and arthritis.

subject: Dermatology
front: What is Erythema Induratum of Bazin, and what is it associated with?
back: A tuberculide — a TB-related panniculitis/vasculitis hypersensitivity reaction.

subject: Dermatology
front: What is erythema marginatum, and what condition is it classically associated with?
back: A rash with pink, serpiginous/ring-like margins on trunk and limbs, classically seen in Acute Rheumatic Fever (ARF).

subject: Dermatology
front: What is the classic lesion morphology of Erythema Multiforme, and what are its major triggers?
back: Target (bull's-eye) lesions; major triggers include HSV (most common), Mycoplasma, sulfa drugs, beta-lactam antibiotics, and chloroquine.

subject: Dermatology
front: What is "bull's eye maculopathy," and what causes it?
back: A retinal finding of concentric pigmentary rings around the macula, caused by chloroquine (antimalarial) retinal toxicity.

subject: Dermatology
front: What causes erythema migrans, how is it transmitted, and what is its treatment?
back: Caused by Lyme disease (Borrelia burgdorferi), transmitted by Ixodes tick bite (history of trekking); drug of choice is Doxycycline.

subject: Dermatology
front: What is erythema ab igne, and what causes it?
back: A reticulate, hyperpigmented erythema caused by chronic exposure to heat (e.g., heating pads, laptops) rather than infection.

subject: Dermatology
front: What is pyoderma gangrenosum, and which IBD subtype is it more strongly associated with?
back: A neutrophilic, ulcerating skin disease; more strongly associated with Ulcerative Colitis than Crohn's disease.

subject: Dermatology
front: Does IBD-associated erythema nodosum/pyoderma gangrenosum reliably improve with treatment of the underlying IBD?
back: No — the source marks this relationship with 'XX' (the same shorthand used elsewhere in these notes to denote 'none/absent'), indicating no reliable response to IBD treatment.

subject: Dermatology
front: What is Erythema Gyratum Repens, and what is it associated with?
back: A rare figurate erythema with a "wood-grain" pattern; strongly paraneoplastic, most often linked to underlying adenocarcinoma.

subject: Dermatology
front: What is the classic distribution pattern of Pityriasis Rosea on the trunk?
back: "Christmas tree" pattern, following skin cleavage lines.

subject: Dermatology
front: What is the "Herald patch" in Pityriasis Rosea, and how does it appear?
back: The initial, largest lesion that precedes the generalized eruption; shows a collarette of scale resembling cigarette paper at its margin.

subject: Dermatology
front: What is the causative organism of Pityriasis Rosea, and what is its treatment?
back: Human Herpesvirus 6/7 (HHV-6/7); treatment is conservative (self-limiting).

subject: Dermatology
front: What is the most common causative organism of Pityriasis Versicolor?
back: Malassezia globosa (a Malassezia species).

subject: Dermatology
front: What is the mechanism behind hypopigmented lesions in Pityriasis Versicolor?
back: Malassezia produces azelaic acid which inhibits melanocyte tyrosinase activity causing hypopigmentation.

subject: Dermatology
front: What is the mechanism behind hyperpigmented lesions in Pityriasis Versicolor?
back: Increased melanosome production/transfer in the affected skin.

subject: Dermatology
front: Describe the characteristic scale and photosensitivity of Pityriasis Versicolor.
back: Fine "branny" scales; lesions are photosensitive and fail to tan, becoming more visible with sun exposure.

subject: Dermatology
front: What does Wood's lamp examination show in Pityriasis Versicolor?
back: Golden-yellow fluorescence.

subject: Dermatology
front: What is the classic KOH mount appearance in Pityriasis Versicolor?
back: "Spaghetti and meatball" appearance (short hyphae with clusters of yeast/spores).

subject: Dermatology
front: What culture medium and colony appearance is used to identify Malassezia?
back: Sabouraud Dextrose Agar (SDA) overlaid with olive oil; colonies show a "fried egg" appearance.

subject: Dermatology
front: What organism causes Tinea Nigra?
back: Hortaea werneckii (a dematiaceous fungus).

subject: Dermatology
front: What are the technical specifications of a Wood's lamp?
back: UV-A light at 365 nm, produced using a filter of barium silicate plus 9% nickel oxide (NiO).

subject: Dermatology
front: What organisms cause impetigo, and what is its classic appearance?
back: Group A Streptococcus (S. pyogenes) and Staphylococcus aureus; produces "honey-colored crusting".

subject: Dermatology
front: What causes bullous impetigo, and what is the molecular target?
back: Staphylococcus aureus exfoliative toxin, which targets Desmoglein-1 (Dsg-1).

subject: Dermatology
front: Differentiate erysipelas from cellulitis by depth of involvement, organism, and lesion appearance.
back: Erysipelas involves the superficial dermis, usually caused by Streptococcus, presenting as a well-defined, raised, erythematous lesion (positive Millian's ear sign). Cellulitis involves the deeper dermis, is caused by both Group A Strep and Staph, and presents as an ill-defined lesion.

subject: Dermatology
front: What is SSSS/Ritter disease — its target antigen, age group, and mucosal involvement?
back: Staphylococcal Scalded Skin Syndrome, caused by an exfoliative toxin targeting Desmoglein-1; occurs in infants with diffuse skin peeling; oral mucosa is NOT involved (distinguishing it from TEN).

subject: Dermatology
front: What is reactive arthritis (Reiter's disease) — its triad and typical antecedent infections?
back: A seronegative arthritis with conjunctivitis, arthritis, and urethritis; typically follows an STD or GI infection (e.g., Campylobacter, Shigella).

subject: Dermatology
front: What skin/mucosal findings accompany reactive arthritis?
back: Circinate balanitis and keratoderma blenorrhagicum.

subject: Dermatology
front: What is the progression from folliculitis to furuncle to carbuncle?
back: Folliculitis (infection of a single hair follicle) progresses to Furuncle (deeper abscess of a single follicle), which can coalesce into a Carbuncle (multiple furuncles); carbuncles are associated with diabetes.

subject: Dermatology
front: What condition is Scleredema (Scleredema diabeticorum) associated with?
back: Diabetes mellitus.

subject: Dermatology
front: What are Fournier's gangrene and Meleney's gangrene?
back: Both are forms of necrotizing fasciitis — Fournier's gangrene affects the perineal/genital region; necrotizing fasciitis in general is typically polymicrobial.

subject: Dermatology
front: In Fournier's gangrene, are the testes typically involved?
back: No — the testes are typically spared, due to their separate blood supply.

subject: Dermatology
front: What class of drug is a recognized risk factor for Fournier's gangrene/necrotizing fasciitis?
back: SGLT-2 inhibitors (gliflozins).

subject: Dermatology
front: What organism causes erythrasma, and what does Wood's lamp show?
back: Corynebacterium minutissimum; Wood's lamp shows coral-red fluorescence.

subject: Dermatology
front: What are the classic features of candidal intertrigo?
back: Occurs in humid, skin-fold areas; presents with satellite lesions (small pustules/papules surrounding the main lesion).

subject: Dermatology
front: What are the major causes of acanthosis nigricans?
back: Insulin resistance (Diabetes Mellitus, PCOD), paraneoplastic syndrome (associated with adenocarcinoma), and HAIR-AN syndrome.

subject: Dermatology
front: What does HAIR-AN syndrome stand for?
back: HyperAndrogenism, Insulin Resistance, Acanthosis Nigricans.

subject: Dermatology
front: What does SAHA syndrome stand for, and what is its underlying cause?
back: Seborrhea, Acne, Hirsutism, Alopecia — an androgen excess syndrome.

subject: Dermatology
front: What gene/pump defect causes Darier's disease, and what are its nail and skin findings?
back: ATP2A2 gene (SERCA2 calcium-ATPase pump) defect; skin shows greasy "crop-grain" papules; nails show V-shaped nicking.

subject: Dermatology
front: What gene/pump defect causes Hailey-Hailey disease, and what are its nail and histology findings?
back: ATP2C1 gene (Golgi Ca-ATPase pump) defect; nails show longitudinal lines; histology shows a "dilapidated brick wall" pattern of acantholysis.

subject: Dermatology
front: What histological feature is common to both Darier's disease and Hailey-Hailey disease?
back: Acantholysis (loss of keratinocyte cohesion), each due to a distinct calcium-ATPase pump defect.

subject: Dermatology
front: What causes pitted keratolysis, and what factor predisposes to it?
back: Caused by Micrococcus (Kytococcus) species; predisposed to by prolonged moisture/water exposure of the feet.

subject: Dermatology
front: Compare contact dermatitis, candida dermatitis, and perianal streptococcal infection by age group, rash location, appearance, and treatment.
back: Contact dermatitis: infants (most common); spares skin folds; red, irritated skin; treated with barrier ointment/paste. Candida dermatitis: infants (2nd most common); involves skin folds; beefy-red with satellite lesions; treated with topical antifungals. Perianal Streptococcus: school-aged children; perianal/perineal area; bright, sharply demarcated erythema; treated with oral antibiotics.

subject: Dermatology
front: What mnemonic covers the main causes of scarring alopecia, and what is the DOC for one of them?
back: T-L-D: Tinea capitis (DOC: Griseofulvin), Lichen Planus, and Discoid Lupus Erythematosus (DLE).

subject: Dermatology
front: What is the ''footprints in snow'' appearance associated with?
back: Pseudopelade of Brocq, a form of scarring alopecia.

subject: Dermatology
front: What condition, causing a receding hairline with perifollicular scarring, is shown alongside Pseudopelade of Brocq as a scarring alopecia?
back: Focal Fibrosing Alopecia.

subject: Dermatology
front: What causes telogen effluvium, and what is its typical timing?
back: Stress or pregnancy; hair loss typically occurs about 3 months after the triggering event.

subject: Dermatology
front: What causes anagen effluvium?
back: Chemotherapy.

subject: Dermatology
front: What is trichotillomania, and what sign describes the appearance of its irregular bald patch?
back: An OCD-related hair-pulling disorder affecting accessible areas of the scalp; the irregular patch is described by the source as the 'Fair Tuck sign' (likely a variant spelling of the eponymous 'Friar Tuck sign').

subject: Dermatology
front: What histological/clinical features are seen in trichotillomania?
back: Broken hair follicles, hemorrhage, and hairs of varying lengths within the patch; can be complicated by a trichobezoar from hair swallowing (trichophagia).

subject: Dermatology
front: What are the treatment options for androgenetic alopecia?
back: Topical Minoxidil (2% for females, 5% for males), Oral Finasteride (a 5-alpha reductase inhibitor), and anti-androgens (used only in females).

subject: Dermatology
front: Which classification systems are used for male vs female pattern androgenetic alopecia?
back: Hamilton classification for male-pattern baldness; Ludwig classification for female-pattern baldness.

subject: Dermatology
front: What is the pathophysiology of alopecia areata?
back: An autoimmune process directed against hair follicles.

subject: Dermatology
front: What histological and clinical hair findings are characteristic of alopecia areata?
back: "Swarm of bees" appearance (peribulbar lymphocytic infiltrate) on histology; exclamation-mark hairs clinically.

subject: Dermatology
front: What nail finding and unusual hair phenomenon are associated with alopecia areata?
back: Regular nail pitting; and the phenomenon of hair "going white overnight" (rapid shedding of pigmented hairs, sparing white/grey hairs).

subject: Dermatology
front: What is the treatment for alopecia areata?
back: Intralesional steroids for localized disease; systemic steroids for extensive disease.

subject: Dermatology
front: Define alopecia totalis and alopecia universalis.
back: Alopecia totalis = total or almost total loss of scalp hair. Alopecia universalis = loss of all body hair.

subject: Dermatology
front: Define Ophiasis and Sisaipho pattern of alopecia areata.
back: Ophiasis = alopecia along the scalp margin in a serpentine band-like pattern. Sisaipho pattern (reverse ophiasis) = hair loss that spares the sides and back of the head.

subject: Dermatology
front: Which body sites does Trichophyton affect, and what is its characteristic macroconidia shape and hair invasion pattern?
back: Affects skin, nail, and hair; macroconidia are pencil-shaped; causes endothrix infection (fungal elements within the hair shaft), appearing as a 'black dot' pattern.

subject: Dermatology
front: Which body sites does Microsporum affect, and what is its characteristic macroconidia shape, hair invasion pattern, and fluorescence?
back: Affects skin and hair (not nail); macroconidia are spindle-shaped; causes ectothrix infection ('grey patch' pattern) with blue-green fluorescence on Wood's lamp.

subject: Dermatology
front: Which body sites does Epidermophyton affect, and what is its characteristic macroconidia shape?
back: Affects skin and nail (not hair); macroconidia are club/Civatte-body shaped.

subject: Dermatology
front: What is a Kerion, and what are its clinical features?
back: An inflammatory, boggy, tender, pustular form of tinea capitis with enlarged regional lymph nodes; caused by zoophilic dermatophytes such as T. mentagrophytes or T. verrucosum.

subject: Dermatology
front: What is Favus, and what are its characteristic features?
back: A chronic form of tinea capitis with crusting and cup-shaped crusts called 'scutula'; caused by T. schoenleinii; shows dull-green fluorescence on Wood's lamp.

subject: Dermatology
front: What is the hair perforation test used for, and which organism is classically positive?
back: Used to help identify the causative dermatophyte species in vitro; T. mentagrophytes is classically positive.

subject: Dermatology
front: What are the classic clinical/lab features and treatment of Tinea Corporis?
back: Central clearing of the lesion with a positive KOH mount; drug of choice is an azole antifungal.

subject: Dermatology
front: What is Tinea Incognito, and what causes its atypical presentation?
back: A tinea infection with an atypical clinical morphology caused by prior topical steroid use, which masks or modifies the classic ring-like appearance.

subject: Dermatology
front: What is the most common clinical pattern of onychomycosis?
back: Distal Lateral Subungual Onychomycosis (DLSO).

subject: Dermatology
front: What is the drug of choice for onychomycosis, and what is the treatment duration for fingernails vs toenails?
back: Terbinafine; 6 weeks for fingernails, 12 weeks for toenails.

subject: Dermatology
front: Name the topical nail lacquer treatments and other topical agents used for onychomycosis.
back: Nail lacquers: Amorolfine 5%, Ciclopirox olamine 8%. Other topical agents: Tavaborole, Efinaconazole.

subject: Dermatology
front: What organism causes scabies, and what are its key morphological features?
back: Sarcoptes scabiei mite, which has 2 pairs of anterior legs and 2 pairs of posterior legs.

subject: Dermatology
front: What are the classic clinical features and typical distribution of scabies?
back: Intense pruritus with burrows and papules; classically involves interdigital spaces, wrists, and the waist; the face is typically spared in adults.

subject: Dermatology
front: What is the first-line treatment for scabies, and what alternatives are safe in infants/pregnancy?
back: 5% Permethrin is first-line; Sulphur and Permethrin are considered safe in infants and pregnant women.

subject: Dermatology
front: Which anti-scabies treatments are best avoided/contraindicated in special populations such as infants or pregnancy?
back: Benzyl benzoate, Lindane, and Ivermectin.

subject: Dermatology
front: What is the 'Oriental sore' of cutaneous leishmaniasis, and how is it transmitted?
back: A non-healing ulcer with raised edges; transmitted by the bite of the sandfly (Phlebotomus).

subject: Dermatology
front: What causes Cutaneous Larva Migrans (CLM), and what is its classic appearance?
back: Ancylostoma braziliense; produces a serpiginous, creeping eruption that migrates 1-2 cm per day.

subject: Dermatology
front: What causes Visceral Larva Migrans (VLM)?
back: Toxocara canis.

subject: Dermatology
front: What causes 'Larva currens,' and how does its migration speed differ from CLM?
back: Strongyloides stercoralis; migrates much faster than CLM, at 5-15 cm per day.

subject: Dermatology
front: What condition does Onchocerca volvulus cause, how is it transmitted, and what are its features?
back: Causes 'river blindness'; transmitted by blackfly bite; features include nodules, pruritus, 'leopard skin' pigmentary changes, and vision loss.

subject: Dermatology
front: What condition does Loa loa cause, and how is it transmitted?
back: Causes Calabar swelling (a transient, localized angioedema); transmitted by deer fly bite.

subject: Dermatology
front: What causes Demodex-related skin disease, and what does it clinically resemble?
back: Overgrowth of the commensal Demodex mite; produces rosacea-like facial papules.

subject: Dermatology
front: What are the three forms of Pediculosis (lice infestation), and what unique finding is seen with pubic lice?
back: Pediculosis capitis (head lice), Pediculosis corporis (body lice), and Pediculosis pubis (pubic lice); P. pubis can cause 'macula cerulea' (bluish-grey macules at bite sites).

subject: Dermatology
front: What is the Ridley-Jopling spectrum of leprosy, from most resistant to least resistant host immunity?
back: TT (Tuberculoid) -> BT -> BB (mid-borderline) -> BL -> LL (Lepromatous), representing decreasing cell-mediated immunity and increasing bacillary load.

subject: Dermatology
front: How does the number of skin lesions change across the TT to LL spectrum?
back: It increases progressively, from few lesions (often just one) in TT to more than 30 lesions in LL.

subject: Dermatology
front: How do lesion margins change across the TT to LL spectrum?
back: Well-defined, elevated margins in TT progress to ill-defined margins in LL.

subject: Dermatology
front: How does nerve involvement change across the TT to LL spectrum?
back: A single thickened nerve in TT progresses to multiple, bilaterally thickened nerves in LL.

subject: Dermatology
front: How does the Slit Skin Smear (SSS) for AFB change across the TT to LL spectrum?
back: It is negative in TT and becomes positive (AFB+) toward LL.

subject: Dermatology
front: How does sensory loss in lesions change across the TT to LL spectrum?
back: Lesions are markedly anesthetic in TT, while sensation is more preserved toward LL.

subject: Dermatology
front: How does the granuloma type change across the TT to LL spectrum?
back: Tuberculoid granulomas are seen in TT, transitioning to foamy (Virchow) macrophages with a Grenz zone in LL.

subject: Dermatology
front: What is the 'Grenz zone,' and in which form of leprosy is it seen?
back: A zone of normal collagen separating the granulomatous infiltrate from the epidermis; seen in Lepromatous Leprosy (LL).

subject: Dermatology
front: What nerve finding is classically palpable in leprosy?
back: Great auricular nerve thickening.

subject: Dermatology
front: Approximately how many skin lesions are typical for BT, BB, BL, and LL leprosy respectively?
back: BT: 1-3 lesions (often with satellite lesions); BB: 3-10 lesions (geographic, punched-out, 'inverted saucer' appearance); BL: 10-30 lesions; LL: more than 30 lesions.

subject: Dermatology
front: What are the Fernandez and Mitsuda lepromin reactions, and what do they measure?
back: Fernandez reaction (read at 48 hours) is an early reaction; Mitsuda reaction (read at 21 days) is a late reaction reflecting long-term cell-mediated immunity (CMI).

subject: Dermatology
front: What stain is used to detect Mycobacterium leprae, and why?
back: Fite-Faraco stain, a modified acid-fast stain, since M. leprae's lipid-rich cell wall stains poorly with the standard Ziehl-Neelsen technique.

subject: Dermatology
front: What are Histoid, Lucio, and Lazarine leprosy?
back: Histoid leprosy presents with nodules; Lucio leprosy is a diffuse, non-nodular form seen in LL; Lazarine leprosy is seen in malnourished patients with nodulo-ulcerative lesions.

subject: Dermatology
front: According to the Indian classification, which leprosy types have a good prognosis or a distinct presentation?
back: Indeterminate leprosy has a good prognosis; Pure neuritic leprosy is a distinct type with isolated nerve involvement without skin lesions.

subject: Dermatology
front: What is the route of infection for leprosy?
back: Inhalation (via the nasal/respiratory mucosa).

subject: Dermatology
front: Which cranial nerve is most commonly affected in leprosy, and which peripheral nerve is most commonly affected overall?
back: The 7th (facial) nerve is the most commonly affected cranial nerve; the ulnar nerve is the most commonly affected peripheral nerve overall.

subject: Dermatology
front: Which nerves are preferred for nerve biopsy in leprosy?
back: Radial cutaneous nerve or sural nerve.

subject: Dermatology
front: Which sensory modality is lost earliest in leprosy skin lesions?
back: Temperature (cold) sensation.

subject: Dermatology
front: What is the single-dose chemoprophylaxis regimen for contacts of leprosy patients, and who qualifies?
back: Single-dose Rifampicin (SDR), given to contacts aged over 2 years who have had at least 20 hours/week of contact for more than 3 months.

subject: Dermatology
front: What is the WHO/NLEP 'elimination' impact indicator for leprosy, and what other indicator is tracked?
back: Prevalence of less than 1 per 10,000 population defines elimination (achieved in India in 2005); newly diagnosed cases with Grade 2 disability is also tracked as an impact indicator.

subject: Dermatology
front: How is Paucibacillary (PB) leprosy defined vs Multibacillary (MB) leprosy, by skin lesions, nerves, and SSS AFB status?
back: PB: 0-5 skin lesions, 0 nerves involved, SSS AFB negative. MB: more than 5 skin lesions, 1 or more nerves involved, SSS AFB positive.

subject: Dermatology
front: What is the MDT (multi-drug therapy) duration for PB vs MB leprosy?
back: PB: 6 months; MB: 12 months.

subject: Dermatology
front: What are the components and doses of the Uniform MDT regimen used in India's NLEP?
back: Rifampicin 600 mg once a month (supervised); Dapsone 100 mg once daily; Clofazimine 300 mg once a month (supervised) plus 50 mg once daily.

subject: Dermatology
front: Compare Type 1 and Type 2 (ENL) lepra reactions by hypersensitivity type, leprosy type affected, and timing relative to treatment.
back: Type 1 reaction: Type IV hypersensitivity, seen in BB/BT, occurs within about 12 months of starting treatment. Type 2 reaction (Erythema Nodosum Leprosum, ENL): Type III hypersensitivity, seen in LL, has no fixed relationship to treatment timing and can occur anytime.

subject: Dermatology
front: How do the clinical features differ between Type 1 and Type 2 lepra reactions?
back: Type 1: pre-existing lesions become red and inflamed (upgrading/downgrading reaction), without significant systemic involvement. Type 2 (ENL): new, tender, nodular skin lesions with systemic involvement such as fever, arthralgia, and orchitis.

subject: Dermatology
front: How are Type 1 and Type 2 lepra reactions treated, and should MDT be stopped during a reaction?
back: Type 1: first-line NSAIDs, escalating to steroids if needed. Type 2 (ENL): drug of choice is steroids. In both types, MDT should NOT be stopped during a reaction.

subject: Dermatology
front: In urethral/cervical discharge syndrome, which organisms are most commonly responsible, and what is the investigation of choice?
back: Chlamydia trachomatis is more common than Gonorrhea; NAAT (Nucleic Acid Amplification Test) is the investigation of choice.

subject: Dermatology
front: Under India's syndromic STI management kits, what regimen and kit color is used for urethral discharge, cervical discharge, and painful scrotal swelling, and how are partners managed?
back: Kit 1 (Grey): Tab. Azithromycin 1g single dose + Tab. Cefixime 400mg single dose. Partners: treat all recent partners for urethral discharge and scrotal swelling; treat partners only if symptomatic for cervical discharge.

subject: Dermatology
front: What syndromic kit and regimen is used for vaginal discharge syndrome, and how are partners managed?
back: Kit 2 (Green): Tab. Secnidazole 2g stat + Cap. Fluconazole 150mg stat single dose; partners treated only if symptomatic.

subject: Dermatology
front: What syndromic kit/regimen is used for anorectal discharge syndrome?
back: The 'Brown kit': Cefixime 800 mg stat + Doxycycline 100 mg for 7 days.

subject: Dermatology
front: What is the treatment for primary, secondary, or early latent syphilis?
back: Benzathine Penicillin 2.4 MU IM, single dose.

subject: Dermatology
front: What is the treatment for late latent or tertiary syphilis?
back: Benzathine Penicillin 2.4 MU IM, given as 3 weekly doses.

subject: Dermatology
front: What is the treatment for neurosyphilis, and what unique adverse reaction can it cause?
back: Aqueous (Procaine) Penicillin; can cause Hoigne syndrome (an acute psychosis-like reaction, distinct from true penicillin allergy).

subject: Dermatology
front: What is the Jarisch-Herxheimer reaction, and is it a reason to stop penicillin?
back: A reaction due to rapid killing of spirochetes after starting penicillin, causing fever and myalgia; it is NOT a contraindication to continuing penicillin, and is managed with NSAIDs.

subject: Dermatology
front: How is syphilis managed in a pregnant patient with a penicillin allergy?
back: Desensitization to penicillin is performed, since penicillin remains necessary in pregnancy due to reliable transplacental passage.

subject: Dermatology
front: What syndromic kit and regimen is used for non-herpetic genital ulcer disease, and what is the alternative if allergic to penicillin?
back: Kit 3 (White): Inj. Benzathine Penicillin 2.4 MU single dose + Tab. Azithromycin 1g single dose. If allergic to penicillin, use Kit 4 (Blue): Doxycycline 100mg BID for 15 days + Azithromycin 1g single dose. Partners are treated for the past 3 months.

subject: Dermatology
front: What syndromic kit and regimen is used for herpetic genital ulcer disease, and is partner treatment required?
back: Kit 5 (Red): Tab. Acyclovir 400mg TDS for 7 days; no partner treatment is required.

subject: Dermatology
front: What syndromic kit and regimen is used for lower abdominal pain (PID) syndrome, and how are male partners managed?
back: Kit 6 (Yellow): Tab. Cefixime 400mg single dose + Tab. Metronidazole 400mg BID for 14 days + Doxycycline 100mg BID for 14 days; male partners are treated with Kit 1.

subject: Dermatology
front: What syndromic kit and regimen is used for inguinal bubo syndrome, and how are partners managed?
back: Kit 7 (Black): Doxycycline 100mg BID for 21 days + Azithromycin 1g single dose; all sexual partners from the past 3 weeks are treated.

subject: Dermatology
front: What are the key features of HSV genital ulcers (appearance, histology, incubation period)?
back: Multiple painful erosions/vesicles on an erythematous base; multinucleated giant cells and acantholysis on Tzanck smear; incubation period 2-5 days.

subject: Dermatology
front: What are the key features of Chancroid (organism, lymph nodes, gram stain, incubation period)?
back: Caused by Haemophilus ducreyi; painful, suppurative inguinal lymph nodes (bubo); Gram stain shows a 'school of fish' pattern; incubation period 2-5 days.

subject: Dermatology
front: What are the key features of the syphilitic chancre (organism, character, lymph nodes, incubation period)?
back: Caused by Treponema pallidum; a hard, indurated, painless ulcer; bilateral, painless ('shotty') lymphadenopathy; incubation period 9-90 days.

subject: Dermatology
front: What are the key features of Donovanosis/Granuloma Inguinale (organism, appearance, special findings, incubation period)?
back: Caused by Klebsiella granulomatis; a red, 'beefy' ulcer without true lymphadenopathy (may show a subcutaneous 'pseudo-bubo'); Donovan bodies (Miyagawa corpuscles) seen on smear; can progress to genital elephantiasis (esthiomene, saxophone deformity); incubation period 8-80 days.

subject: Dermatology
front: What are the key features of Lymphogranuloma Venereum/LGV (organism, serotype, special signs, incubation period)?
back: Caused by Chlamydia trachomatis (serovar L2 most common); produces only a transient ulcer with prominent bubo formation; classic 'groove sign' (grooving of inguinal/femoral nodes by the inguinal ligament); diagnosed historically via the Frei test; incubation period 3-30 days.

subject: Dermatology
front: What organism causes Bacterial Vaginosis, and what diagnostic criteria/scores are used?
back: Gardnerella vaginalis; diagnosed using Amsel's criteria (clinical) or Nugent's score (Gram stain-based).

subject: Dermatology
front: What is the treatment for Bacterial Vaginosis?
back: Metronidazole or Clindamycin.

subject: Dermatology
front: What examination finding is classic for Trichomonas vaginitis, and what is its treatment?
back: 'Strawberry cervix' appearance; treated with Metronidazole, with treatment of the sexual partner also required.

subject: Dermatology
front: What is the treatment for Candida vaginitis?
back: Fluconazole.

subject: Dermatology
front: What features characterize physiological (normal) vaginal discharge?
back: No odour, no itching, and it typically occurs mid-cycle.

subject: Dermatology
front: What organism is associated with IUCD use, and what characteristic cytological/clinical findings does it produce?
back: Actinomyces; produces a 'cotton-ball/cotton-wool' appearance on cytology, and is linked to a history of IUCD use and pelvic inflammatory disease (PID).

subject: Dermatology
topic: Pemphigus vs Bullous Pemphigoid - Level of Split
front: At what level does Pemphigus cause blistering, what is the bulla character, and what is the target antigen?
back: Intraepidermal split (within the epidermis); flaccid bullae; target antigen is Desmoglein (DSG).

subject: Dermatology
topic: Pemphigus vs Bullous Pemphigoid - Level of Split
front: Differentiate the two main Desmoglein subtypes in Pemphigus by split location and clinical presentation.
back: DSG-1: subcorneal split, causing Pemphigus foliaceus, which can resemble SSSS. DSG-3: suprabasal split with oral ulcers, causing Pemphigus vulgaris, which can resemble SJS-TEN.

subject: Dermatology
topic: Pemphigus vs Bullous Pemphigoid - Level of Split
front: At what level does Bullous Pemphigoid cause blistering, what is the bulla character, and which BP antigen is more important?
back: Subepidermal (dermo-epidermal junction) split; tense bullae; BP antigen 2 (BP180) is more important than BP antigen 1 (BP230).

subject: Dermatology
topic: Pemphigus vs Bullous Pemphigoid - Level of Split
front: What is Epidermolysis Bullosa, and what are its two acquired/inherited forms?
back: A mechano-bullous disorder; EB Congenita (inherited) and EB Acquisita (autoimmune, targeting Type VII collagen).

subject: Dermatology
front: What is the Nikolsky sign (tangential pressure), and in which conditions is it positive?
back: Gentle tangential pressure on skin causes shearing/blistering of the epidermis; positive in Pemphigus, SJS-TEN, and SSSS.

subject: Dermatology
front: What is the Asboe-Hansen sign (bulla spread sign, lateral pressure), and in which condition is it positive?
back: Lateral pressure on an intact bulla causes it to spread into adjacent skin; positive in Pemphigus.

subject: Dermatology
front: In salt-split skin indirect immunofluorescence, what does 'roof' staining indicate versus 'floor' staining?
back: Roof staining means the target antigen is on the epidermal side, as in Bullous Pemphigoid; Floor staining means the antigen is on the dermal side, as in Epidermolysis Bullosa Acquisita.

subject: Dermatology
front: Which drugs can cause drug-induced Pemphigus?
back: D-penicillamine, Captopril, and Rifampicin.

subject: Dermatology
front: What malignancy is classically associated with paraneoplastic pemphigus?
back: Non-Hodgkin Lymphoma (NHL) (flag: source notation also mentions 'CML/CLL' alongside NHL — verify exact association against original notes).

subject: Dermatology
front: What is the first-line bedside test and the investigation of choice (IOC) for Pemphigus Vulgaris?
back: Tzanck smear (taken from the floor of the blister) is first-line; Direct Immunofluorescence (DIF) showing IgG/C3 in an intercellular 'fish-net' pattern is the investigation of choice.

subject: Dermatology
front: What is the treatment of choice for Pemphigus Vulgaris?
back: Steroids (often given as pulse therapy).

subject: Dermatology
front: What are the clinical features of Bullous Pemphigoid (base, itching, blood findings)?
back: Tense bullae on an erythematous base; marked itching; associated peripheral eosinophilia.

subject: Dermatology
front: What does DIF show in Bullous Pemphigoid?
back: Linear IgG/C3 deposition at the dermo-epidermal junction (DEJ).

subject: Dermatology
front: What is the classic clinical sign in Linear IgA Disease, and where are lesions typically distributed?
back: 'String of pearls' sign; lesions are typically peri-orificial.

subject: Dermatology
front: What does DIF show in Linear IgA Disease, and what is its treatment?
back: Linear IgA deposition at the DEJ; treated with Dapsone.

subject: Dermatology
front: What are the clinical features and key disease association of Dermatitis Herpetiformis?
back: Intense itching, typically on extensor surfaces; strongly associated with Celiac disease.

subject: Dermatology
front: What does DIF show in Dermatitis Herpetiformis, and what is its treatment?
back: Granular IgA deposition at the dermal papillary tips ('picket fence' pattern); treated with Dapsone.

subject: Dermatology
front: What is Herpes Gestationis (Pemphigoid Gestationis), and how does it relate to Bullous Pemphigoid?
back: A pregnancy-associated autoimmune bullous disease that is considered a variant related to Bullous Pemphigoid.

subject: Dermatology
front: What other bullous condition shares the BP antigen 2 (BP180) target, alongside certain forms of Linear IgA disease?
back: Cicatricial pemphigoid.

subject: Dermatology
front: What drug causes flagellate pigmentation, and what does it look like?
back: Bleomycin; produces whip-like (flagellate), linear streaks of hyperpigmentation.

subject: Dermatology
front: What drug causes 'ceruloderma' (blue-grey skin discoloration)?
back: Amiodarone.

subject: Dermatology
front: What drug causes livedo reticularis as a side effect?
back: Amantadine.

subject: Dermatology
front: What type of hypersensitivity reaction is Fixed Drug Eruption (FDE), what are its most common causes, and what does it leave behind after healing?
back: Type IV hypersensitivity; most commonly caused by NSAIDs (and metronidazole); heals with residual hyperpigmentation at the same site upon re-exposure.

subject: Dermatology
front: How are SJS and TEN differentiated by body surface area (BSA) involvement?
back: SJS involves less than 10% BSA; TEN involves more than 30% BSA (10-30% is SJS-TEN overlap).

subject: Dermatology
front: What are the major causative drugs for SJS/TEN?
back: Antiepileptic drugs (e.g., Carbamazepine, Lamotrigine), Allopurinol, NSAIDs, and Sulfa drugs.

subject: Dermatology
front: What is SCORTEN, and what is it used for?
back: 'Score of Toxic Epidermal Necrolysis' -- a prognostic severity scoring system for TEN.

subject: Dermatology
front: What is the classic drug-infection combination that causes a morbilliform (measles-like) rash?
back: Infectious mononucleosis (EBV) combined with penicillin (classically ampicillin/amoxicillin).

subject: Dermatology
front: What does DRESS stand for?
back: Drug Reaction with Eosinophilia and Systemic Symptoms.

subject: Dermatology
front: What causes Red Man Syndrome, and what is its mechanism?
back: Vancomycin, via histamine release (typically due to rapid infusion).

subject: Dermatology
front: What causes Grey Baby Syndrome?
back: Chloramphenicol (due to immature neonatal hepatic glucuronidation).

subject: Dermatology
front: What drugs cause pseudo-jaundice (without true hyperbilirubinemia)?
back: Rifabutin and beta-carotene.

subject: Dermatology
front: What antiretroviral drug causes skin/nail hyperpigmentation?
back: Zidovudine.

subject: Dermatology
front: What antiretroviral drug causes palm/sole pigmentation?
back: Emtricitabine.

subject: Dermatology
front: What drugs cause hand-foot syndrome (palmar-plantar erythrodysesthesia)?
back: 5-Fluorouracil (5-FU) and oral Capecitabine.

subject: Dermatology
front: What drug causes purple toe syndrome?
back: Warfarin.

subject: Dermatology
front: What drug causes pseudolymphoma and purple glove syndrome?
back: Phenytoin.

subject: Dermatology
front: What class of drug causes vesicular eruptions as a cutaneous adverse effect?
back: Barbiturates (CNS depressants).

subject: Dermatology
front: What drug causes ichthyosis-like skin changes and copper/orange-brown discoloration?
back: Clofazimine.

subject: Dermatology
front: What mediates the flushing reaction seen with Niacin?
back: Prostaglandin D2 (PGD2) release.

subject: Dermatology
front: What are the two main types of contact dermatitis?
back: Irritant contact dermatitis and Allergic contact dermatitis.

subject: Dermatology
front: What is the patch test used for, and at what time points is it read?
back: Used to identify the allergen causing allergic contact dermatitis; read at 48 hours and 96 hours.

subject: Dermatology
front: What type of hypersensitivity reaction underlies allergic contact dermatitis?
back: Type IV (delayed-type/cell-mediated) hypersensitivity.

subject: Dermatology
front: What causes Airborne Contact Dermatitis (ABCD), and what is the responsible allergen?
back: Parthenium (Congress grass); the responsible allergen is sesquiterpene lactone.

subject: Dermatology
front: What is the most common cause of allergic contact dermatitis, and where is it typically encountered?
back: Nickel, most commonly from artificial jewellery.

subject: Dermatology
front: What metal/compound found in cement causes allergic contact dermatitis?
back: Chromium (potassium dichromate).

subject: Dermatology
front: What chemical found in bindi adhesive causes contact dermatitis?
back: PTBP (para-tertiary-butylphenol).

subject: Dermatology
front: What chemical found in hair dyes causes contact dermatitis?
back: PPD (para-phenylenediamine).

subject: Dermatology
front: What topical medication ingredient commonly causes contact dermatitis?
back: Neomycin.

subject: Dermatology
front: What chemical found in rubber products causes contact leucoderma?
back: Monobenzyl ether of hydroquinone (MBEH).

subject: Dermatology
front: Describe the acute, subacute, and chronic clinical stages of atopic dermatitis.
back: Acute: erythema, intercellular edema (spongiosis), vesicles, and crusting. Subacute: erythema and scaling. Chronic: lichenification.

subject: Dermatology
front: What criteria are used to diagnose atopic dermatitis?
back: Hanifin and Rajka criteria (major features include a chronic course, personal/family history of atopy, pruritus, and typical distribution).

subject: Dermatology
front: What cytokines and hypersensitivity type drive atopic dermatitis?
back: Th2 response with IL-4 and IL-5; classified as Type I hypersensitivity.

subject: Dermatology
front: List the characteristic periorbital/facial signs associated with atopic dermatitis.
back: Dennie-Morgan fold (infraorbital fold), shield-like cataract, keratoconus, and the 'headlight sign' (perialar pallor with nasal sparing).

subject: Dermatology
front: What are the treatment options for atopic dermatitis, including two targeted agents?
back: Topical/systemic steroids and calcineurin inhibitors are mainstays; Crisaborole (a PDE4 inhibitor) and Dupilumab (an IL-4 receptor-blocking biologic) are targeted options.

subject: Dermatology
front: What is the pathophysiology and hypersensitivity classification of ordinary urticaria?
back: Dermal edema causing pruritic, transient wheals with dermographism; classified as Type I hypersensitivity.

subject: Dermatology
front: What triggers cholinergic urticaria?
back: Sweating (e.g., from heat, exercise, or emotional stress).

subject: Dermatology
front: What clinical sign and molecular marker characterize cutaneous mastocytosis?
back: Darier's sign (localized urtication when a lesion is rubbed) and C-KIT (CD117) positivity/mutation.

subject: Dermatology
front: How does Hereditary Angioedema (HAE) differ from typical histamine-mediated urticaria/angioedema?
back: HAE shows no wheals and is NOT histamine-mediated; it is inherited in an autosomal dominant pattern.

subject: Dermatology
front: What is the underlying biochemical defect in Hereditary Angioedema, and what are the characteristic lab findings?
back: C1 esterase inhibitor deficiency, leading to elevated bradykinin and low C4 levels.

subject: Dermatology
front: What are the treatment options for Hereditary Angioedema?
back: Plasma kallikrein inhibitors (Ecallantide, Lanadelumab, Berotralstat), the bradykinin B2 receptor antagonist Icatibant, and historically Danazol for prophylaxis.

subject: Dermatology
front: What is the basic pathogenesis of acne?
back: Obstruction of the pilosebaceous unit, with or without secondary infection by Cutibacterium (Propionibacterium) acnes.

subject: Dermatology
front: Differentiate open and closed comedones.
back: Open comedones ('blackheads') are open to the skin surface with oxidized sebum causing the black color; closed comedones ('whiteheads') are covered by a thin layer of epidermis.

subject: Dermatology
front: List the acne lesion types in order of increasing severity.
back: Comedones, then Papules, then Pustules, then Nodulocystic lesions.

subject: Dermatology
front: What is the stepwise treatment ladder for acne based on lesion type?
back: Comedones: topical retinoids (Adapalene/Tretinoin). Papules: add a topical antibiotic (Clindamycin). Pustules: add an oral antibiotic (Doxycycline) plus benzoyl peroxide. Nodulocystic acne: oral Isotretinoin.

subject: Dermatology
front: What are the key side effects/precautions of oral Isotretinoin?
back: Teratogenic (pregnancy must be avoided for about 3 months after stopping); can cause cheilitis, raised triglycerides, and hepatotoxicity.

subject: Dermatology
front: In cases of resistant acne, what underlying condition should be ruled out?
back: Hyperandrogenism.

subject: Dermatology
front: What are the distinguishing features of drug-induced acne compared to typical acne?
back: Lesions are monomorphic and characteristically lack comedones.

subject: Dermatology
front: Which drugs are classically implicated in drug-induced acne?
back: Steroids (which also cause dermal atrophy) and Lithium.

subject: Dermatology
front: How is rosacea distinguished from acne?
back: Rosacea shows erythema and telangiectasia but characteristically has NO comedones, unlike acne.

subject: Dermatology
front: What triggers flushing in rosacea?
back: Response to triggers such as hot beverages and alcohol.

subject: Dermatology
front: How does the malar rash of SLE help distinguish it from rosacea on the face?
back: SLE's malar rash characteristically spares the nasolabial folds, whereas rosacea typically involves them.

subject: Dermatology
front: How do freckles (ephelides) differ from lentigines regarding sun exposure, and what conditions is each associated with?
back: Freckles (ephelides) increase in number/darkness with sun exposure and are associated with Xeroderma Pigmentosum and NAME syndrome. Lentigines do NOT change with sun exposure and are associated with Peutz-Jeghers syndrome.

subject: Dermatology
front: What are the causes of Melasma (Chloasma)?
back: Pregnancy and thyroid disease.

subject: Dermatology
front: What is the 'CHIK sign,' and what infection is it associated with?
back: A characteristic facial (perioral/nasal) pigmentation pattern seen in Chikungunya infection.

subject: Dermatology
front: What is Becker's nevus?
back: A hyperpigmented patch, often with hypertrichosis, typically found on the shoulder/upper trunk.

subject: Dermatology
front: How do you differentiate epidermal from dermal pigmentation clinically?
back: Epidermal pigmentation is brown and is enhanced by Wood's lamp examination; Dermal pigmentation is blue/slate-grey, shows the Tyndall effect, and is not enhanced by Wood's lamp.

subject: Dermatology
front: Name three examples of dermal pigmentary lesions.
back: Mongolian spots, Nevus of Ota, and Nevus of Ito.

subject: Dermatology
front: What is the enzyme defect and inheritance pattern of oculocutaneous albinism?
back: Tyrosinase deficiency; autosomal recessive (AR) inheritance.

subject: Dermatology
front: What are the characteristic features of Nevus Depigmentosus?
back: Congenital and non-progressive; caused by a defect in melanin distribution (not melanocyte number); shows satellite lesions and feathery margins.

subject: Dermatology
front: What is the inheritance pattern and gene mutation of Piebaldism, and what is its characteristic pattern?
back: Autosomal dominant; C-KIT gene mutation; shows an 'island of sparing' pattern with a white forelock, due to absent melanocytes from a neural crest cell migration defect.

subject: Dermatology
front: What is the inheritance pattern, gene mutation, and hallmark clinical sign of Waardenburg syndrome?
back: Autosomal dominant; PAX3 gene mutation; hallmark finding is heterochromia iridis (also with white forelock).

subject: Dermatology
front: What is Nevus Anemicus, and what is its underlying mechanism?
back: A functional (not truly pigmentary) vascular anomaly caused by alpha-1 receptor-mediated vasoconstriction, producing a pale patch.

subject: Dermatology
front: What is the underlying pathophysiology of vitiligo?
back: Autoimmune destruction of melanocytes.

subject: Dermatology
front: List the clinical subtypes of vitiligo.
back: Focal, Segmental, Acro-facial, Vulgaris, and Universalis.

subject: Dermatology
front: What is distinctive about segmental vitiligo's course?
back: It follows a dermatomal distribution, tends to grow initially, and then becomes stable.

subject: Dermatology
front: Which vitiligo subtypes carry a poorer prognosis?
back: Acro-facial and Universalis vitiligo.

subject: Dermatology
front: What are the poor prognostic factors in vitiligo overall?
back: Long-standing disease, involvement over bony prominences, leukotrichia, and lip-tip involvement.

subject: Dermatology
front: What is the treatment for vitiligo?
back: Topical steroids for localized disease; systemic steroids or calcineurin inhibitors for more extensive disease.

subject: Dermatology
front: What is the inheritance pattern and gene mutation in Incontinentia Pigmenti?
back: X-linked dominant (XLD); NEMO gene mutation.

subject: Dermatology
front: What mnemonic covers the classic X-linked dominant conditions, and what does it stand for?
back: 'R A V I' -- Rett syndrome, Aicardi syndrome, Vitamin D-resistant (hypophosphatemic) rickets, and Incontinentia pigmenti.

subject: Dermatology
front: What are the sequential skin stages of Incontinentia Pigmenti?
back: Vesicular stage, then Verrucous stage, then Hyperpigmented (whorled/marble-cake) stage, then Hypopigmented/atrophic stage.

subject: Dermatology
front: What are Blaschko's lines, and what do they represent?
back: Lines that follow the pattern of embryological skin cell migration; used to explain the distribution of mosaic skin conditions (e.g., Incontinentia Pigmenti).

subject: Dermatology
front: What are Langer's lines, and what is their clinical significance?
back: Lines corresponding to the natural orientation of dermal collagen fibers; traditionally used to guide surgical skin incisions.

subject: Dermatology
front: What are Kraissl's lines, and how do they differ from Langer's lines?
back: Relaxed skin tension lines used for planning surgical incisions to optimize cosmetic outcome, as an alternative to Langer's lines.

subject: Dermatology
front: Describe the clinical appearance and histology of a Junctional Nevus.
back: A flat, uniformly pigmented macule; histologically shows nests of melanocytes at the dermo-epidermal junction.

subject: Dermatology
front: Describe the clinical appearance and histology of a Compound Nevus.
back: A slightly elevated, uniformly pigmented papule; histologically shows nests of melanocytes at both the dermo-epidermal junction and within the dermis.

subject: Dermatology
front: Describe the clinical appearance and histology of an Intradermal Nevus.
back: A dome-shaped papule that is flesh-colored or lightly pigmented; histologically, melanocytes are located entirely within the dermis.

subject: Dermatology
front: What are the clinical features of a Congenital Melanocytic Nevus (CMN), and what is the malignancy risk threshold for giant variants?
back: Present at birth, may have hair, and large variants carry a malignancy risk; a giant CMN (greater than 20 cm) has an increased risk of malignant transformation.

subject: Dermatology
front: Describe the clinical appearance and histology of a Halo Nevus.
back: A central pigmented nevus surrounded by a depigmented halo; histologically shows lymphocytic infiltration around the nevus cells.

subject: Dermatology
front: Describe the clinical appearance and histology of a Dysplastic (Atypical) Nevus.
back: Irregular border and color variation, may resemble melanoma clinically; histologically shows architectural disorder, cytologic atypia of melanocytes, and bridging of rete ridges.

subject: Dermatology
front: What are the clinical features of Actinic Keratosis, and is it premalignant?
back: Presents as a scaly lesion in photo-exposed areas; it IS premalignant, with potential to progress to squamous cell carcinoma.

subject: Dermatology
front: What is the classic appearance of Seborrheic Keratosis, and what paraneoplastic sign is associated with sudden multiple lesions?
back: A 'stuck-on' appearance; sudden eruption of multiple lesions is called the Sign of Leser-Trelat, a paraneoplastic marker associated with adenocarcinoma.

subject: Dermatology
front: Is a Cutaneous Horn/Keratoacanthoma premalignant?
back: No, it is NOT considered premalignant.

subject: Dermatology
front: What is the most common skin cancer, and what is its classic clinical appearance?
back: Basal Cell Carcinoma (BCC); presents as a 'rodent ulcer' with rolled-out, pearly margins.

subject: Dermatology
front: What is the characteristic histology of BCC?
back: True palisading of basaloid cells at the periphery of tumor nests.

subject: Dermatology
front: What are the treatment options for BCC?
back: Vismodegib (a Sonic Hedgehog/SHH pathway inhibitor) and Mohs micrographic surgery.

subject: Dermatology
front: What are the major risk factors for Squamous Cell Carcinoma (SCC)?
back: Sun exposure, older age, immunosuppression, chronic wounds, burns, and arsenic exposure.

subject: Dermatology
front: What is the characteristic histological finding in SCC?
back: Keratin pearls.

subject: Dermatology
front: What are the four major clinical types of melanoma, and which is most common worldwide vs in Asians?
back: Superficial spreading (most common worldwide), Lentigo maligna (radial growth phase), Nodular (vertical growth phase), and Acral lentiginous (most common in Asians).

subject: Dermatology
front: What is the single most important prognostic factor in melanoma?
back: Breslow depth (tumor thickness).

subject: Dermatology
front: What is the most common anatomical site for melanoma in India, and what mutations are relevant?
back: Extremities are the most common site in India; BRAF (V600E) and CDKN2A mutations are relevant.

subject: Dermatology
front: What targeted drug is used to treat BRAF-mutated melanoma?
back: Vemurafenib.

subject: Dermatology
front: What is the natural course of Infantile Hemangioma, and what are its classic descriptive names?
back: Typically undergoes spontaneous regression; also known as 'strawberry' hemangioma or 'stork bite' depending on location/type.

subject: Dermatology
front: What is a Cherry Angioma, and does it regress spontaneously?
back: A capillary hemangioma occurring in adults; does NOT involute spontaneously.

subject: Dermatology
front: What are the clinical features of a Glomus Tumor, and what is its physiological role?
back: Presents as a painful, red lesion; glomus bodies normally play a role in thermoregulation.

subject: Dermatology
front: What is 'pyoderma gravidarum,' and when does it occur?
back: A pyogenic granuloma-type vascular lesion occurring during pregnancy.

subject: Dermatology
front: What causes Bacillary Angiomatosis, in which patient population is it seen, and what stain confirms it?
back: Caused by Bartonella henselae; seen in HIV-positive patients; confirmed with Warthin-Starry stain; presents as violaceous vascular lesions.

subject: Dermatology
front: What is Stewart-Treves syndrome?
back: Development of lymphangiosarcoma arising in an area of chronic lymphedema present for many years.

subject: Dermatology
front: What causes Kaposi Sarcoma, in which patient population is it seen, and what is its treatment?
back: Caused by HHV-8; seen in HIV-positive patients; treated with alpha-interferon.

subject: Dermatology
front: What other conditions besides Kaposi Sarcoma are caused by HHV-8?
back: Castleman's disease and Primary effusion lymphoma.

subject: Dermatology
front: What is the heliotrope rash, and what condition is it associated with?
back: A violaceous (purple) erythema of the eyelids/periorbital region; a classic sign of Dermatomyositis.

subject: Dermatology
front: What are Gottron's papules?
back: Scaly, violaceous papules over the extensor surfaces of the knuckles/interphalangeal joints; a pathognomonic sign of Dermatomyositis.

subject: Dermatology
front: What is the 'Shawl sign' in Dermatomyositis?
back: Erythema in a shawl-like distribution over the upper back, shoulders, and V of the neck, in sun-exposed areas.

subject: Dermatology
front: What other nail-fold finding is seen in Dermatomyositis?
back: Periungual telangiectasias.

subject: Dermatology
front: What is a tuberculide, and what is an example?
back: A hypersensitivity reaction to TB antigens rather than direct skin infection; example: Lichen Scrofulosorum (a Type IV hypersensitivity reaction).

subject: Dermatology
front: What is Scrofuloderma, and in which age group is it most common?
back: A form of cutaneous TB arising from direct extension from underlying tuberculous lymphadenitis/bone; most common cutaneous TB in children.

subject: Dermatology
front: What is Lupus Vulgaris, and what are its key features?
back: The most common cutaneous TB in adults; shows apple jelly nodules on diascopy; typically paucibacillary with AFB-negative smears; skin biopsy shows granuloma.

subject: Dermatology
front: What conditions are classically associated with central scarring, central clearing, and central crusting patterns of skin lesions?
back: Central scarring: cutaneous TB (Lupus vulgaris). Central clearing: Tinea. Central crusting ('volcano sign'): Post Kala-azar Dermal Leishmaniasis (PKDL).

subject: Dermatology
front: What is the inheritance pattern, chromosome, and gene for NF1?
back: Autosomal dominant; chromosome 17; Neurofibromin gene.

subject: Dermatology
front: What is the inheritance pattern, chromosome, and gene for NF2, and what is its key clinical finding?
back: Autosomal dominant; chromosome 22; Merlin gene; classic finding is bilateral vestibular schwannoma (also ependymoma and meningioma, as part of MISME syndrome).

subject: Dermatology
front: What is the inheritance pattern, chromosomes/genes, and treatment for Tuberous Sclerosis Complex (TSC)?
back: Autosomal dominant; chromosome 9 (Hamartin) and chromosome 16 (Tuberin); treated with mTOR inhibitors such as Everolimus.

subject: Dermatology
front: What is the inheritance pattern, chromosome, and key associated tumors of Von Hippel-Lindau (VHL) syndrome?
back: Autosomal dominant; chromosome 3; associated with clear cell renal cell carcinoma, pheochromocytoma, and hemangioblastoma.

subject: Dermatology
front: What is the inheritance pattern, chromosome/gene, and key features of Sturge-Weber Syndrome (SWS)?
back: Sporadic; chromosome 9, GNAQ gene; features include 'tram-track' intracranial calcifications, port-wine stain (V1 distribution most common), and congenital glaucoma.

subject: Dermatology
front: What is the inheritance pattern, chromosome, and key features of Ataxia-Telangiectasia (ATM)?
back: Autosomal recessive; chromosome 11; features include ataxia and telangiectasia.

subject: Dermatology
front: List the diagnostic criteria for NF1.
back: Six or more cafe-au-lait macules (over 5mm in prepubertal children, over 15mm in postpubertal individuals); axillary or inguinal freckling (Crowe sign); two or more neurofibromas of any type or one plexiform neurofibroma; optic pathway glioma; two or more Lisch nodules (iris hamartomas); sphenoid dysplasia or tibial pseudoarthrosis/cortical bone lesion; a first-degree relative with NF1.

subject: Dermatology
front: What descriptive terms are used for the cafe-au-lait macule borders and associated bony signs in NF1?
back: The macule borders are described as 'Coast of California' (smooth borders); associated bony signs include the button-hole sign and bare orbit sign.

subject: Dermatology
front: List the major diagnostic features of Tuberous Sclerosis Complex (TSC).
back: Facial angiofibromas, hypomelanotic (ash leaf) macules, shagreen patches, cortical tubers, subependymal nodules, subependymal giant cell tumors, retinal hamartomas, cardiac rhabdomyomas, renal angiomyolipomas, and pulmonary lymphangioleiomyomatosis (LAM).

subject: Dermatology
front: List the minor diagnostic features of Tuberous Sclerosis Complex (TSC).
back: 'Confetti' skin lesions, gingival fibromas, dental enamel pits, cerebral white matter radial migration lines, retinal achromatic patches, bone cysts, and hamartomatous rectal polyps.

subject: Dermatology
front: What causes Beau's lines?
back: Transverse grooves in the nail indicating a temporary arrest of nail growth, due to any significant systemic illness or stress.

subject: Dermatology
front: What causes Mees' lines?
back: Arsenic poisoning.

subject: Dermatology
front: What causes Muehrcke's bands?
back: Malnutrition/hypoalbuminemia.

subject: Dermatology
front: What is another name for Lindsay nails, and what condition are they associated with?
back: Also called 'half-and-half' or '50-50' nails; associated with renal failure.

subject: Dermatology
front: What condition is associated with Terry's nails?
back: Liver failure (cirrhosis).

subject: Dermatology
front: What is 'salt-and-pepper pigmentation,' and in what condition is it seen?
back: Mixed hyper- and hypopigmented mottling of the skin; seen in Scleroderma.

subject: Dermatology
front: What are the classic sites of Seborrheic Dermatitis?
back: Scalp and nasolabial folds.

subject: Dermatology
front: Name four discoid/patterned skin conditions grouped together for comparison in the notes.
back: Discoid/Nummular Eczema, Discoid Lupus Erythematosus (DLE), Salt-Pepper Pigmentation (Scleroderma), and Seborrheic Dermatitis.

subject: Dermatology
front: What are the key features of Lamellar Ichthyosis?
back: Presents with a membrane and scales covering the trunk at birth (collodion baby); caused by epidermal transglutaminase-1 deficiency; associated with ectropion.

subject: Dermatology
front: What are Collodion baby and Harlequin baby?
back: Severe congenital presentations of ichthyosis at birth: Collodion baby (a shiny, taut membrane covering the skin) and Harlequin baby (the most severe form, with thick, plate-like scales).

subject: Dermatology
front: What is the enzyme defect in X-linked recessive (XLR) Ichthyosis, and where do scales typically occur?
back: Steroid sulfatase deficiency; scales typically occur on the trunk.

subject: Dermatology
front: What are the features of Pityriasis Alba, and how does facial Indeterminate Leprosy differ from it?
back: Pityriasis Alba is scaly, itchy, and associated with atopy. Indeterminate Leprosy causing facial hypopigmentation additionally shows sensory loss, which Pityriasis Alba does not.

subject: Dermatology
front: What symptom is characteristically associated with genital Lichen Sclerosus?
back: Dyspareunia.

subject: Dermatology
front: What are the typical features of Dermatitis Artefacta?
back: Self-inflicted skin lesions, typically found on accessible areas reachable by the patient's non-dominant hand.

subject: Dermatology
front: What is Morphea, and what dermoscopic sign is associated with it?
back: Localized scleroderma; associated with the 'Box sign' on dermoscopy.

subject: Dermatology
front: What is the classic triad of Netherton Syndrome, and what gene is mutated?
back: Bamboo hair (trichorrhexis invaginata), Atopic dermatitis, and Ichthyosis (ichthyosis linearis circumflexa); caused by mutation in the SPINK5 gene.

subject: Dermatology
front: What hair finding is characteristic of Trichothiodystrophy, and what does the PIBIDS acronym stand for?
back: 'Tiger tail' hair pattern on polarized microscopy; PIBIDS stands for Photosensitivity, Ichthyosis, Brittle hair, Intellectual impairment, Decreased fertility, and Short stature.

subject: Dermatology
front: Which HPV types cause plantar warts?
back: HPV types 1 and 2.

subject: Dermatology
front: Which HPV types cause Verruca vulgaris (common warts)?
back: HPV types 2, 4, and 27.

subject: Dermatology
front: Which HPV types cause Verruca plana (flat warts)?
back: HPV types 3 and 10.

subject: Dermatology
front: Which HPV types cause Focal epithelial hyperplasia (Heck's disease)?
back: HPV types 13 and 32.

subject: Dermatology
front: Which HPV types cause Condyloma acuminata (genital warts)?
back: HPV types 6 and 11.

subject: Dermatology
front: Which HPV types are considered high-risk (oncogenic)?

subject: Dermatology
front: What are the treatment options for HPV-related warts, and which are considered safe in pregnancy?
back: Podophyllin, Imiquimod (a TLR-7 agonist), trichloroacetic acid, and cryotherapy; trichloroacetic acid and cryotherapy are considered safe in pregnancy, while podophyllin and imiquimod are generally avoided.

subject: Dermatology
front: What preservative is noted as a contact allergen alongside HPV wart treatments in the source material?
back: Methylisothiazolinone, a common preservative found in cosmetic/personal care products.

subject: Dermatology
front: How does microconidia abundance differ across Trichophyton, Microsporum, and Epidermophyton?
back: Trichophyton: abundant microconidia (++); Microsporum: few microconidia (+/-); Epidermophyton: no microconidia (-).

subject: Dermatology
topic: Pemphigus vs Bullous Pemphigoid - Level of Split
front: What are the three major categories of Epidermolysis Bullosa (EB), and what molecular target/level does each involve?
back: EB Simplex — targets Keratin 5/14, at the epidermis level. Junctional EB — targets Integrin and Laminin 332 (also linked to BP180), at the basement membrane zone. Dystrophic EB — targets Type VII collagen, at the dermis level.

subject: Dermatology
front: What is the characteristic scale pattern of Ichthyosis Vulgaris, and how common is it relative to other ichthyoses?
back: A fine, 'fish-net' (reticulate) scale pattern; it is the most common type of ichthyosis overall.
